# gardenOS Companion — master development strategy

After re-evaluating the companion-app discussions together with the wider gardenOS Core/Server/Node work and the Nandi/agricultural robotics material, I would expand the original concept substantially.

**gardenOS Companion should become the universal human interface to the gardenOS ecosystem**, not merely a native replacement for the ESP web interface.

Your own robotics specification already anticipates GPS/RTK navigation, multiple coordinated ground vehicles, aerial-drone mapping, fleet-management software and remote diagnostics. fileciteturn1file0L51-L72 The broader project roadmap also deliberately progresses from remote control → assisted navigation → sensor fusion/AI → swarm deployment. fileciteturn1file7L621-L629

That changes how I would build the app.

---

# 1. Recommended architecture

The target ecosystem should become:

```text id="uofddm"
                         OPTIONAL CLOUD
                              │
                     ┌────────┴────────┐
                     │ gardenOS Cloud │
                     └────────┬────────┘
                              │ encrypted
                              │
                    ┌─────────▼─────────┐
                    │  gardenOS Server  │
                    │  Site/Farm Edge   │
                    └──────┬─────┬─────┘
                           │     │
             ┌─────────────┘     └─────────────┐
             │                                 │
       gardenOS Core                     ROBOTICS LAYER
             │                                 │
      ┌──────┴───────┐              ┌──────────┼──────────┐
      │              │              │          │          │
    Node           Node          Nandi 01   Nandi 02    Drone
      │              │              │          │          │
 Sensors/        Relays/         sensors    tools       camera
 actuators       pumps           RTK/GPS                mapping

                 ▲
                 │
       ┌─────────┴──────────┐
       │ gardenOS Companion │
       │                    │
       │ iPhone             │
       │ iPad               │
       │ Android phone      │
       │ Android tablet     │
       └────────────────────┘
```

The crucial architectural rule is:

> **The app supervises the system. It must not itself become the safety-critical controller.**

Motor stabilization, collision avoidance, E-stop handling, geofence enforcement, communications-loss behaviour, pump safety and drone failsafes belong on the hardware/controller/vehicle.

This follows the direction already present in the rover proposal: start with manual plus assisted navigation, preserve safety-stop functionality, operate offline and introduce autonomy progressively after basic mobility has been proven. fileciteturn1file6L531-L567

---

# 2. Flutter remains my recommendation — with an important qualification

I re-evaluated Flutter against native Swift/Kotlin and other cross-platform options.

I would still choose:

**Flutter + native platform integrations**

rather than three independent applications.

Current Flutter supports a single codebase across Android and iOS, with platform-specific Swift/Kotlin integration available where required. ([docs.flutter.dev](https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration?utm_source=chatgpt.com)) Current Flutter 3.47 supports Android API 24–37 and iOS 15–26. ([docs.flutter.dev](https://docs.flutter.dev/reference/supported-platforms?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

But I would **not** attempt to implement the entire robotics stack in Dart.

Instead:

```text id="oomczz"
Flutter
│
├── UI
├── state management
├── dashboards
├── maps
├── configuration
├── missions
├── fleet interface
├── Core management
└── normal garden automation
       │
       ▼
Native integration layer
│
├── iOS: Swift
├── Android: Kotlin
├── MAVSDK bridge
├── BLE / accessory discovery
├── local networking
├── video
└── hardware-specific integrations
```

This gives gardenOS the maintainability of one application while leaving an escape hatch for robotics libraries.

---

# 3. Four connection modes

The companion application should understand four fundamentally different situations.

| Mode | App connects to | Intended use |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct Core** | gardenOS Core | Home garden / single controller |
| **Direct Vehicle** | Nandi/robot/drone | Setup, testing, field service |
| **Site Mode** | gardenOS Server | Farm + multiple Core units + fleet |
| **Remote Mode** | Server through secure relay/cloud | Remote monitoring/control |

This is particularly important.

A home user should **not need gardenOS Server**.

Their system can remain:

```text id="ldkiu8"
Phone
  │
Wi-Fi
  │
gardenOS Core
  │
Nodes
```

Your existing Core philosophy already supports standalone operation, configuration backups, automation presets, OTA and a browser UI. fileciteturn1file1L138-L164

A farm might instead have:

```text id="0jckqz"
                    gardenOS Server
                   /      |       \
                 /        |        \
             Core 1     Core 2    Fleet
               │          │       / | \
             Nodes       Nodes   R1 R2 D1
```

The same Companion app controls both.

---

# 4. gardenOS Server becomes much more important

For irrigation alone, Server can be optional.

For **fleet operation**, it becomes the preferred architecture.

The phone should not coordinate five robots because:

- iOS/Android may suspend the application.
- Wi-Fi connections disappear.
- batteries die.
- users walk away.
- incoming calls and OS conditions occur.
- a mobile device shouldn't be the authoritative scheduler.

So:

### gardenOS Server should own

```text id="5vvfq4"
Site state
Mission queue
Robot task allocation
Fleet positions
Maps
Geofences
RTK correction source/bridge
Telemetry history
Alerts
Device registry
User permissions
Automation
Mission logs
Charging state
Maintenance records
```

The phone becomes the operator console.

---

# 5. The app information architecture

I would make the main navigation something like:

```text id="mbbxj5"
gardenOS

OVERVIEW
│
├── Home / Site
├── Alerts
└── Activity

GARDEN
│
├── Zones
├── Plants
├── Irrigation
├── Environment
└── Automation

FLEET
│
├── Map
├── Vehicles
├── Missions
├── Tasks
└── Charging

DEVICES
│
├── Core
├── Nodes
├── Sensors
├── Actuators
└── Gateways

DATA
│
├── History
├── Maps
├── Reports
└── Logs

SYSTEM
│
├── Automation
├── Integrations
├── Firmware
├── Backups
└── Settings
```

The interface should change dynamically.

A user with one Core and no robot should **never see an intimidating robotics console**.

A commercial farm with four Nandis and two drones gets the Fleet section automatically.

---

# 6. Fleet management

This is where the previous companion-app concept needs the largest expansion.

A fleet view should show:

```text id="ru7nct"
NANDI FLEET                    10:42

● Nandi 01     WEEDING
  Battery 82%
  ETA 24 min
  RTK FIX
  █████████░

● Nandi 02     CHARGING
  Battery 43%
  Dock A
  ETA 1h 12m

● Nandi 03     AVAILABLE
  Battery 96%

● Survey 01    DRONE
  Mapping field B
  Battery 67%

─────────────────────────────

Map
┌───────────────────────────┐
│      Field A              │
│  R1 → → →                 │
│                           │
│             R3            │
│                           │
│      Field B       D1 ✈   │
└───────────────────────────┘

[ + New Mission ]
```

For a small local fleet, Companion should support approximately:

**1–20 vehicles initially.**

Nothing prevents later expansion, but designing for hundreds of autonomous machines would unnecessarily complicate the first architecture.

---

# 7. Vehicle abstraction

Do not make the app know every individual motor-controller implementation.

Create a common gardenOS vehicle model:

```text id="subi5d"
Vehicle
├── identity
├── type
│    ├── rover
│    ├── tractor
│    ├── drone
│    └── stationary
│
├── pose
├── velocity
├── heading
├── battery
├── connectivity
├── navigation state
├── capabilities
├── payload/tool
├── mission
├── safety state
└── telemetry
```

Capabilities can advertise themselves.

Example:

```json id="vkiqo9"
{
  "vehicleId": "nandi-03",
  "type": "rover",
  "capabilities": [
    "navigate",
    "rtk",
    "camera",
    "tow",
    "cultivate",
    "soil_scan"
  ]
}
```

The UI then generates suitable controls automatically.

That supports your modular-machine philosophy far better than hardcoding every Nandi variant.

---

# 8. Implements should be first-class devices

This will matter enormously later.

The app should understand that:

```text id="qwsfur"
Nandi
   +
Cultivator
```

is operationally different from:

```text id="b0p3uw"
Nandi
   +
Sprayer
```

or:

```text id="zrfg14"
Nandi
   +
Sensor mast
```

The underlying project already calls for a universal mount, power/data interface and interchangeable sprayer, seeder, sensor, cargo and weeding payloads. fileciteturn1file6L527-L558

So create:

```text id="gkfd9h"
Vehicle
   │
   └── Tool
        ├── identity
        ├── capabilities
        ├── operating limits
        ├── calibration
        ├── service hours
        └── consumables
```

Then Companion can display:

```text id="hyke8g"
Nandi 02

Tool:
Rotary Cultivator

Working width: 650 mm
Depth: 80 mm
Status: READY
Hours: 18.6

Recommended speed:
0.4–0.8 m/s
```

---

# 9. Missions rather than direct driving

Most routine interaction should be mission-oriented.

Example:

```text id="k8h7m1"
MISSION

Field: Vegetable Field 2
Vehicle: Auto select
Task: Cultivate

Area:
████████████████

Spacing: 600 mm
Speed: 0.6 m/s

Avoid:
☑ Trees
☑ Irrigation
☑ Human zones

When complete:
Return to charging station

[ Validate ]

[ Start Mission ]
```

The server chooses the appropriate vehicle.

Eventually:

```text id="dpv3m3"
Task
     ↓
Scheduler
     ↓
Capability matching
     ↓
Vehicle assignment
     ↓
Route planning
     ↓
Execution
```

That is the beginning of actual fleet orchestration.

---

# 10. Manual rover control

There should still be a manual control page.

But the app should send something like:

```text id="nitn3i"
requested_velocity:
  linear: 0.35
  angular: -0.12
```

not:

```text id="br9j05"
left_motor_pwm = 136
right_motor_pwm = 204
```

The robot owns its drivetrain.

And manual driving needs:

```text id="5ag4e8"
Hold-to-drive / dead-man control
Connection-loss stop
Local E-stop
App emergency stop
Speed limiting
Obstacle override protection
Geofence
Operator presence
Command timeout
```

If control packets stop, the rover stops.

No exceptions.

---

# 11. Drone integration

I would not invent a gardenOS drone protocol.

Use **MAVLink + MAVSDK**.

MAVSDK is specifically intended to manage MAVLink drones/vehicles from ground stations and mobile devices, supports one or multiple vehicles and provides telemetry, missions, movement/action APIs and other controls. It currently supports iOS and Android. ([mavsdk.mavlink.io](https://mavsdk.mavlink.io/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That makes the logical architecture:

```text id="7pko0a"
gardenOS Companion
        │
gardenOS vehicle API
        │
 MAVSDK / MAVLink bridge
        │
      Drone
        │
 ┌──────┴──────┐
 │ PX4/ArduPilot│
 └─────────────┘
```

I would **not expose raw MAVLink throughout the gardenOS application**.

Keep it behind an adapter.

That means gardenOS can later support a different vehicle protocol without rewriting the UI.

---

# 12. Drone control should primarily be mission based

Example:

```text id="48gcu5"
DRONE MISSION

Survey Field 3

Altitude       40 m
Overlap        75%
Side overlap   70%
Speed          6 m/s

Camera:
RGB Survey Cam

Area:
┌─────────────────────┐
│ ↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔        │
│ ↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔        │
│ ↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔↔        │
└─────────────────────┘

Estimated:
Flight       11:32
Distance     4.7 km
Battery      48%

[ Upload ]
[ Start ]
```

The drone's autopilot handles actual flight stability.

MAVSDK's mission system already provides mission and telemetry primitives, while its action system handles operations such as arming/takeoff/landing. ([mavsdk.mavlink.io](https://mavsdk.mavlink.io/main/en/cpp/guide/telemetry.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

# 13. Robotics stack

For Nandi's higher-end onboard computer, I recommend designing around:

**ROS 2 compatibility.**

Not necessarily putting ROS on every cheap rover immediately.

The Community Nandi can use a lighter vehicle agent.

But the advanced platform should be able to expose:

```text id="qarro2"
ROS 2
│
├── drivetrain
├── IMU
├── GPS
├── RTK
├── camera
├── LiDAR/depth
├── obstacle detection
├── navigation
├── tool controller
├── diagnostics
└── autonomy
```

ROS 2 currently uses an abstract middleware layer with DDS implementations such as Fast DDS and Cyclone DDS and also supports non-DDS middleware including Zenoh. ([docs.ros.org](https://docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/Installation/RMW-Implementations.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

However:

### Do NOT connect the Flutter app directly to the ROS graph.

Instead:

```text id="fhi9fu"
ROS 2
  │
gardenOS Robot Agent
  │
gardenOS Protocol
  │
Server / Companion
```

This protects us from:

- ROS version changes
- DDS discovery complexity
- multicast issues
- enormous topic sets
- vendor differences
- mobile-platform networking restrictions

---

# 14. OpenRMF — learn from it, don't adopt all of it yet

I also reviewed OpenRMF.

Its fleet-adapter architecture is extremely relevant. Fleet adapters translate high-level task assignments into implementation-specific robot commands while feeding robot state back to the fleet manager. ([github.com](https://github.com/open-rmf/rmf_ros2/blob/main/rmf_fleet_adapter_python/README.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That is almost exactly the abstraction gardenOS eventually needs:

```text id="j8y9gn"
gardenOS Scheduler
      │
      │ generic task
      ▼
Vehicle Adapter
      │
      ├── Nandi adapter
      ├── MAVLink adapter
      ├── third-party rover
      └── future robot
```

But I **wouldn't install full OpenRMF in v1**.

For 2–10 farm robots it is probably unnecessary complexity.

Instead, imitate its good architectural principle.

If gardenOS eventually operates tens/hundreds of heterogeneous autonomous machines, integration with or migration toward OpenRMF becomes reasonable.

---

# 15. Network protocol strategy

I would formalize several layers.

| Connection | Recommended protocol |
|---|---|
| Companion ↔ Core | HTTP/REST + realtime WebSocket |
| Companion ↔ Server | HTTPS + WebSocket |
| Server ↔ Core | REST/WebSocket or MQTT |
| Server ↔ Robot Agent | MQTT/Protobuf or similar persistent transport |
| Companion ↔ direct robot | gardenOS vehicle API |
| Robot internal | ROS 2 |
| Drone internal | MAVLink |
| Video | WebRTC |
| Device discovery | mDNS / Bonjour |
| Core ↔ hardware Nodes | existing field bus / RS-485 direction |
| Internet remote access | TLS through Server/Cloud |

REST handles things like:

```text id="xezy5k"
GET device
GET configuration
POST rule
POST mission
POST calibration
```

WebSocket handles:

```text id="r3wnqy"
telemetry
vehicle position
sensor updates
mission state
alerts
events
```

Video should remain independent.

---

# 16. gardenOS API v1

This should be created **before the mobile application becomes large**.

Suggested namespaces:

```text id="j6s86l"
/api/v1/

system/
sites/
devices/
nodes/
sensors/
actuators/
zones/
plants/
automation/
alerts/

vehicles/
fleet/
missions/
tasks/
tools/
maps/
geofences/
telemetry/

users/
permissions/

firmware/
backup/
diagnostics/
```

Then:

```text id="qj9rfu"
GET /api/v1/vehicles
```

might return:

```json id="4y6fk9"
[
  {
    "id": "nandi-01",
    "name": "Nandi 01",
    "class": "rover",
    "state": "working",
    "battery": 82,
    "position": {
      "lat": -26.0,
      "lon": 28.0
    },
    "mission": "mission-241"
  }
]
```

The app never needs to know what CPU is inside it.

---

# 17. Keep compatibility with the existing Core API

Don't rewrite functioning firmware unnecessarily.

The existing Core already contains:

```text id="ebtfnd"
browser UI
Wi-Fi/AP management
HTTP/JSON handlers
LittleFS persistence
plant data
rules
automation
OTA
```

fileciteturn1file5L448-L477

So implement a compatibility layer:

```text id="mf8zsz"
OLD

/api/status
/api/rules
/api/garden
/api/device

         ↓ internally mapped ↓

NEW

/api/v1/system/status
/api/v1/automation/rules
/api/v1/garden
/api/v1/devices/core
```

Eventually the old interface can disappear, but not now.

---

# 18. Device discovery

Use:

**mDNS / Bonjour**

with something such as:

```text id="8rozbx"
_gardenos._tcp.local
```

Each device advertises:

```text id="s1j7or"
name
device type
device UUID
API version
firmware
capabilities
```

iOS requires permission for local-network access, and Bonjour service types should be declared in the app configuration. ([developer.apple.com](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3179-understanding-local-network-privacy?changes=__3&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Android is moving in the same direction: Android 17 introduces an `ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK` runtime permission for apps targeting API 37 that discover or communicate with LAN devices. ([developer.android.com](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/Manifest.permission?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So this abstraction should be implemented now rather than relying on IP scanning.

---

# 19. Provisioning needs to change

One area I would change from current Core.

The existing development firmware intentionally uses an open `GardenOS-Setup` AP. fileciteturn1file1L181-L191 The project's own documentation correctly warns not to expose the open setup AP/controller to the public Internet. fileciteturn1file3L373-L379

That is fine for prototypes.

It shouldn't be the production onboarding architecture.

I recommend each production Core/robot gets a QR label containing:

```text id="al49te"
Device ID
Setup token
Public-key fingerprint
Optional setup Wi-Fi credentials
```

Then:

```text id="hapbj4"
Scan QR
   ↓
Connect
   ↓
Verify device identity
   ↓
Select farm/home Wi-Fi
   ↓
Provision credentials
   ↓
Exchange certificates
   ↓
Device joins gardenOS
```

BLE-assisted provisioning can be added where hardware allows it.

---

# 20. Security model

For a pump controller, weak authentication is inconvenient.

For a 300 kg autonomous rover, it is unacceptable.

gardenOS therefore needs device identity from the beginning.

I recommend:

```text id="zz1mxc"
Unique device UUID
Unique cryptographic identity
QR onboarding
TLS
certificate/key rotation
role-based access
command auditing
signed firmware
signed OTA packages
encrypted secret storage
secure remote relay
```

Roles might become:

```text id="am8vm4"
Owner
Administrator
Operator
Technician
Viewer
```

A Viewer can observe telemetry.

A Technician can calibrate a sensor.

An Operator can launch approved missions.

Only appropriate roles can change geofences, disable safety systems or update firmware.

---

# 21. Safety architecture

This part should be designed into the API now.

Every vehicle should report something equivalent to:

```text id="11rtcb"
safetyState:
  NORMAL
  CAUTION
  STOPPED
  ESTOP
  FAULT
```

The application should clearly separate:

```text id="2fkwvl"
STOP MISSION
```

from:

```text id="9fj71w"
EMERGENCY STOP
```

Emergency stopping should operate at multiple levels:

```text id="ohj3wk"
Physical E-stop
        ↓
Vehicle safety controller

App E-stop
        ↓
Vehicle agent
        ↓
Safety controller

Site E-stop
        ↓
Server
        ↓
Entire fleet
```

A network failure must **not be capable of defeating the local E-stop**.

---

# 22. Lost communications

Every rover should have autonomous communications-loss policy.

Example:

```text id="24fsrc"
No command 500 ms:
manual motion stops

Server lost 5 s:
mission pauses

Server lost 30 s:
return / stop safely according to mission policy

Localization invalid:
stop

Geofence violation:
stop

E-stop:
immediate hardware shutdown
```

The exact timings will depend on the eventual machine.

But the architecture belongs onboard.

---

# 23. Video

For robots/drones, include live camera views.

Use WebRTC rather than forcing camera video through the general telemetry connection.

Example iPad layout:

```text id="gzw6p0"
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Nandi 01                         ● ONLINE   │
├──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┤
│                      │ Battery       72%    │
│     LIVE CAMERA      │ RTK           FIX    │
│                      │ Speed       0.6 m/s  │
│                      │ Mission       WEED   │
├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ MAP                  │ Tool                 │
│                      │ Rotary Weeder        │
│        ● N01         │                      │
│   ───────▶           │ [Pause] [Stop]       │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
```

---

# 24. Mapping becomes a core feature

The app should eventually store layers rather than a simple Google/Apple map.

A farm map might contain:

```text id="0yr6rr"
Property
Field boundaries
Beds
Crop rows
Buildings
Roads
Trees
Irrigation
Water lines
Power
Charging stations
No-go zones
Drone zones
Rover zones
Hazards
RTK base
gardenOS Core units
Sensors
```

That map becomes shared context between:

**irrigation + automation + rover + drone + user.**

This is where gardenOS can become genuinely interesting as a unified agricultural system.

---

# 25. Drone-generated maps

Drone imagery should eventually update:

```text id="443s8n"
crop health
weed areas
water stress
planting gaps
field boundaries
terrain
```

Then gardenOS can create rover tasks.

For example:

```text id="51ux65"
Drone surveys Field 2
        ↓
gardenOS identifies suspected weed zones
        ↓
operator reviews
        ↓
Create Weed Mission
        ↓
Nandi executes mission
        ↓
completion map stored
```

That's a far more powerful architecture than separately controlling a drone and a rover.

---

# 26. Automation can eventually include machines

Your current Core already has automation concepts such as Balanced, Water Saver and moisture-sensitive behaviour. fileciteturn1file1L193-L209

Extend the same philosophy:

```text id="vkxuf9"
IF
Field 2 soil moisture < 20%

AND
Rain forecast probability < threshold

THEN
Irrigation Zone 2

AND AFTER
schedule Nandi soil survey
```

Later:

```text id="o2qbtb"
IF
drone vegetation scan indicates anomaly

THEN
create inspection task

AND
assign available Nandi rover
```

This is where gardenOS Server becomes the central orchestration engine.

---

# 27. Offline-first remains essential

This is not merely a nice feature.

Your agricultural robotics plan explicitly calls for offline operation and simple interfaces. fileciteturn1file6L551-L554

Therefore:

```text id="7el4ch"
No Internet
      ≠
gardenOS unavailable
```

A farm LAN should continue operating.

```text id="codkbt"
Internet offline

Phone
  │
Wi-Fi
  │
gardenOS Server
  ├── Core
  ├── Nodes
  ├── Rovers
  └── Drones
```

All local functionality continues.

Cloud should add:

```text id="p2be9n"
remote access
backup
optional analytics
fleet history synchronization
notifications
multi-site management
```

—not basic operation.

---

# 28. iPhone versus iPad

The same application, different UX.

### iPhone

Optimize for:

```text id="41dlbl"
quick status
alerts
basic controls
single vehicle
camera
manual rover driving
mission approval
device setup
```

### iPad/tablet

Turn it into a **field command console**:

```text id="7mdiuh"
fleet map
multi-camera
mission planning
drag/drop task allocation
field maps
graphs
multi-Core overview
maintenance
automation editor
```

Apple itself recommends that iPhone apps work on iPad whenever practical. ([developer.apple.com](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

# 29. HomeKit / Matter

I would change the strategic role of HomeKit.

Do **not** make HomeKit the primary gardenOS protocol.

Use it as an optional consumer integration layer:

```text id="vfooxb"
gardenOS
   │
   ├── Apple Home
   ├── Matter
   ├── Home Assistant
   └── MQTT
```

The existing ESP8266 implementation already demonstrates why: full HomeKit increases memory and network load. fileciteturn1file2L247-L264

For Core installations:

**gardenOS API is authoritative.**

HomeKit/Matter is convenience.

Robots should generally not appear as ordinary HomeKit switches.

---

# 30. App Store implications of vehicle control

Apple explicitly calls out location-based autonomous control of vehicles/aircraft and limits how Location Services should be used; lightweight drones/toys are treated differently. ([developer.apple.com](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That strengthens the architectural decision to have:

```text id="aohmvn"
phone → mission/supervision

rather than

phone GPS → autonomous navigation controller
```

For actual drone deployments, aviation rules need to be treated as deployment requirements rather than simply software features.

For example, SACAA currently states that South African non-private/commercial UAS operations fall under Part 101 requirements, including aircraft/operator approvals and registration requirements. ([caa.co.za](https://www.caa.co.za/industry-information/uas/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So the app should ultimately support configurable jurisdictional/compliance features rather than assuming one country's flight rules.

# 31. Recommended software repository structure

I would create something approximately like:

```text id="qt7was"
gardenos/
│
├── core-firmware/
│
├── node-firmware/
│
├── server/
│
├── robot-agent/
│   ├── core/
│   ├── ros2/
│   ├── mavlink/
│   └── simulator/
│
├── companion/
│   ├── lib/
│   │   ├── api/
│   │   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── discovery/
│   │   ├── garden/
│   │   ├── devices/
│   │   ├── fleet/
│   │   ├── missions/
│   │   ├── maps/
│   │   ├── telemetry/
│   │   ├── video/
│   │   ├── automation/
│   │   └── settings/
│   │
│   ├── ios/
│   └── android/
│
├── protocol/
│   ├── openapi/
│   ├── protobuf/
│   └── schemas/
│
├── simulator/
│
└── docs/
```

Keeping `/protocol` separate is especially important.

The protocol must outlive any one app implementation.

# 32. Build a simulator very early

This will accelerate development enormously.

Create fake:

```text id="mqj2qk"
gardenOS Core
Nandi rover
Drone
weather
soil sensors
battery
missions
faults
```

Then Companion development doesn't need physical machines connected constantly.

You could simulate:

```text id="s0s851"
Nandi 01
Battery 62%
RTK FIX
0.5 m/s
Mission 48%

Nandi 02
Battery 12%
FAULT: LEFT MOTOR

Drone 01
Airborne
Battery 43%
```

and build/test the fleet interface immediately.

---

# 33. Revised development roadmap

I would now divide Companion development into six major generations:

| Generation | Deliverable |
|---|---|
| **0.1** | App shell + Core discovery + current Core monitoring |
| **0.2** | Full Core control/config/rules/backups/OTA |
| **0.3** | Multi-Core + gardenOS Server + site dashboard |
| **0.4** | First Nandi rover + telemetry + manual control + maps |
| **0.5** | Missions + tools + local 2–5 rover fleet |
| **0.6** | Drone/MAVSDK + imagery + combined fleet |
| **0.7** | Assisted navigation + RTK + mission scheduler |
| **0.8** | Automation between garden/fleet systems |
| **0.9** | Remote connectivity + permissions + production security |
| **1.0** | Public iOS/iPadOS/Android release |
| **2.x** | advanced fleet/autonomy/swarm features |

This sequence deliberately matches the existing Nandi philosophy of proving remote/manual mobility before progressively introducing autonomy. fileciteturn1file6L537-L567

---

# 34. What I would build first

The first development target should therefore be considerably more disciplined than simply recreating the current webpage in Flutter.

### gardenOS Companion 0.1

Build:

```text id="zosjor"
Flutter application

iPhone
iPad
Android phone
Android tablet

        ↓

gardenOS Discovery

        ↓

gardenOS API compatibility layer

        ↓

Current gardenOS Core
```

Initial screens:

```text id="yozakt"
Welcome / onboarding
Device discovery
Site selection
Overview
Garden
Zones
Automation
Devices
Alerts
Settings
```

But underneath it, establish the models for:

```text id="vxy6ty"
Site
Device
Core
Node
Sensor
Actuator
Vehicle
Tool
Mission
Task
Map
Geofence
Alert
Telemetry
```

even if Vehicle/Mission aren't shown in 0.1.

That prevents us from having to rewrite the entire application when Nandi is connected.

# 35. Then connect the first Nandi very early

I would **not wait for Companion to be “finished.”**

As soon as the Core app works:

```text id="5chzqv"
Companion 0.4 prototype
       +
Nandi prototype
```

Implement only:

```text id="tgknsv"
discover vehicle
connect
battery
GPS position
heading
speed
camera
manual driving
E-stop
diagnostics
```

Then:

```text id="m6dyeh"
waypoint
route
simple mission
```

Then two rovers.

That gives us real fleet requirements from actual hardware instead of designing everything theoretically.

---

# 36. Store launch

Flutter lets us maintain one application while building native iOS and Android targets. ([docs.flutter.dev](https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Current direct store costs include:

**Apple Developer Program: US$99/year.** ([developer.apple.com](https://developer.apple.com/get-started/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Google's developer registration remains a **US$25 one-time fee** for full distribution, with identity verification requirements. ([support.google.com](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14659200?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

But I would not prioritize either store immediately.

Development progression should be:

```text id="piy47g"
local dev builds
        ↓
internal iPhone/Android testing
        ↓
Nandi prototype testing
        ↓
TestFlight / Android testing
        ↓
small farm pilot
        ↓
public stores
```

---

# 37. The key strategic change

Originally we could reasonably describe Companion as:

> “A mobile interface for gardenOS Core.”

I don't think that's the right product anymore.

It should be:

> **gardenOS Companion — the local and remote control, monitoring, mapping and fleet-management interface for the gardenOS agricultural automation ecosystem.**

With:

```text id="jv45yv"
                         gardenOS
                            │
          ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
          │                 │                 │
        GROW             AUTOMATE          MOVE
          │                 │                 │
        Core              Server            Nandi
        Nodes             Rules             Rovers
        Sensors           Data              Drones
        Water             AI                Tools
          │                 │                 │
          └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                            │
                    gardenOS Companion
```

And perhaps the most important design principle for the entire project becomes:

**Core operates without Server.  
Vehicles operate safely without the app.  
Server operates without the Internet.  
Companion gives the human one coherent interface to everything.**

That architecture is considerably stronger, scales from a single home greenhouse to a small autonomous farm fleet, and remains consistent with your project's original affordability/modularity/repairability objectives. The Nandi material explicitly defines those machines as modular, upgradeable, energy-efficient and suitable for locally maintainable deployment, so the software architecture should follow the same principles. fileciteturn1file0L100-L117 memcite
